entities.summary: Babur (1504–1747) was a Turco-Mongol conqueror and founder of the Mughal Empire, one of history's greatest imperial dynasties. Born in Andijan (modern Uzbekistan), he descended from Timur and Genghis Khan, inheriting a legacy of Central Asian conquest. After losing his ancestral territories to the Uzbeks, Babur turned southward, seizing Kabul in 1504 and using it as a base for repeated invasions of the Indian subcontinent. His decisive victory at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) shattered the Delhi Sultanate's power and established Mughal rule across northern India—a dominion that would endure for two centuries and shape the cultural and political landscape of South Asia. Babur's reign transformed the region through architectural patronage, Persian administrative systems, and a cosmopolitan court that blended Central Asian, Persian, and Indian traditions. His legacy extended far beyond his lifetime: the Mughal Empire he founded became a beacon of Islamic governance, fostering remarkable achievements in art, literature, mathematics, and urban planning. The Durrani Empire that succeeded him in Afghanistan carried forward his vision of Central Asian-South Asian synthesis. Babur remains a towering figure in Islamic and world history—a military genius whose ambitions reshaped empires and whose descendants would rule India for generations.
